title: How does static behave in inheritance?
shortTitle: How does static behave in inheritance?
keyPoints: Static methods are NOT overridden – they are hidden. The method called depends on the reference type, not the object type
Static fields are also hidden, not overridden – a subclass can declare the same-named static field, creating two separate fields
@Override does not work on static methods – the compiler rejects it
Static methods are resolved at compile time (early binding), instance methods at runtime (late binding/polymorphism)
Understanding this concept is essential for Java interviews at senior level

s1_definition.oneliner: Static methods and fields are hidden, not overridden. The call is resolved by the reference type at compile time, not by the object type at runtime. There is no polymorphism for statics.
s1_definition.profdef:
Static inheritance rules:

- **Static methods are hidden.** A subclass can define a static method with the same signature as the parent's. But the call is resolved by the reference type, not the object type. This is hiding, not overriding.
- **No polymorphism.** `Parent p = new Child(); p.staticMethod()` calls Parent's version because the reference type is Parent.
- **@Override is rejected.** The compiler does not allow `@Override` on a static method because it cannot be overridden.
s1_definition.analogy: Each bank branch (subclass) can post its own rate card (static method) on its wall. But when the head office (parent reference) looks up a rate, it reads its own wall, not the branch's. The branch's card is independent, not a replacement.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Instance method: overriding (runtime dispatch)
    Bank b = new SavingsBank();
    b.getName()  → "Savings Division" (object type wins)

  Static method: hiding (compile-time dispatch)
    Bank b = new SavingsBank();
    b.getType()  → "GENERIC" (reference type wins)

  Rule:
    instance → polymorphic (object type)
    static   → NOT polymorphic (reference type)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Static methods and fields are hidden, not overridden. When a subclass defines a static method with the same signature as the parent, the call is resolved by the reference type at compile time, not by the object type at runtime. This means `Bank b = new SavingsBank(); b.getType()` calls Bank's version, not SavingsBank's.

This is fundamentally different from instance methods, which are resolved by the actual object type at runtime (polymorphism). If you need behavior that varies by subclass, use instance methods, not static.

One sentence to remember: static methods are hidden, not overridden – they are resolved by the reference type at compile time with no polymorphism.
